blocks.text: A state government has ₦2 billion. It can build a general hospital, or tar a rural road, or renovate forty classrooms. It builds the hospital. The true cost of that hospital is not ₦2 billion — it is the road that will now stay untarred.

blocks.markdown:
Money cost tells you how many naira left your hand. **Opportunity cost** tells you what you actually gave up. Because resources are scarce, choosing one thing always means refusing something else, and economists treat that refused alternative as the real cost of the decision.

Notice the word *next*. Opportunity cost is not the total of everything you did not choose. It is only the single best alternative you had to drop.

blocks.title: Opportunity cost
blocks.text: The next best alternative forgone when a choice is made. It is also called real cost or alternative forgone, and it is measured in terms of the thing sacrificed, not necessarily in money.

rows: A student with one free evening
blocks.caption: Opportunity cost is always the single highest-ranked alternative dropped

blocks.markdown:
### The production possibility curve

At the level of a whole economy, opportunity cost is shown by a **production possibility curve (PPC)**, sometimes called a transformation curve. It plots the maximum combinations of two goods a country can produce when all its resources are fully and efficiently employed.

The curve slopes downwards from left to right: to get more cloth the country must release resources from cassava, so cassava output falls. It also bows outwards from the origin, because resources are not equally suited to both uses — as more and more land and labour are switched to cloth, each extra unit of cloth costs *more* cassava than the one before. That is the law of increasing opportunity cost.

headers: Cassava given up for the extra cloth
blocks.caption: Each move down the schedule sacrifices 20 tonnes of cassava but buys fewer and fewer extra bales of cloth

items: A point **on** the curve: resources fully and efficiently employed.
A point **inside** the curve: resources under-utilised, for example widespread unemployment or idle factories.
A point **outside** the curve: unattainable with present resources and technology.
The whole curve **shifting outward**: economic growth, caused by more resources, better skills or improved technology.
The whole curve **shifting inward**: loss of productive capacity, for example after a war, flood or mass emigration of skilled workers.

blocks.title: Calculating opportunity cost in money terms
blocks.prompt: A farmer has 5 hectares. Each hectare yields maize worth ₦400,000, or yam worth ₦550,000, or cassava worth ₦300,000. He plants the whole farm with maize. What is the opportunity cost of his decision?

steps.text: List the value of each alternative use of all 5 hectares. Maize: 5 × ₦400,000 = ₦2,000,000.
The best alternative he rejected is yam, because ₦2,750,000 is greater than ₦1,500,000. Cassava is not counted — opportunity cost uses only the NEXT best alternative.
So the opportunity cost of planting maize is the yam output worth ₦2,750,000.

blocks.answer: ₦2,750,000 — the value of the yam harvest forgone

blocks.title: Two marks students lose every year
blocks.text: First, never add up all the rejected alternatives — count only the next best one. Second, when asked for the opportunity cost, name the alternative itself ("the sewing machine") rather than the sum of money spent. Examiners mark the money answer wrong.

points: Opportunity cost is the next best alternative forgone when a choice is made.
It is a real cost measured in sacrificed alternatives, not necessarily in naira.
The production possibility curve shows the combinations of two goods attainable with full employment of resources.
The curve bows outward because opportunity cost increases as resources are switched between uses.
Points inside the curve mean under-utilised resources; an outward shift of the curve means economic growth.
